one_line_reason: The only real single-ingredient human evidence is a branded slow-release L-cysteine lozenge for smoking cessation, with a marginal effect tied to that specific delivery form; the rest of the shortlist is NAC used in unrelated clinical/procedural/biomarker contexts.

selected.population: cigarette smokers (2 RCTs pooled: 423 and 1,998 subjects)
selected.intervention: slow-release L-cysteine lozenge (Acetium®) vs placebo lozenge
selected.dose_as_stated: not stated (delivered as a lozenge; specific mg dose not given in abstract)
selected.why_selected: The only shortlisted trial testing L-cysteine as the primary single-ingredient exposure in a general population; both RCTs trended favorable but only the larger study approached statistical significance (OR 1.26, 95% CI 0.99-1.59)

blockers: The mechanism (locally neutralizing salivary acetaldehyde) is specific to a slow-release lozenge held in the mouth, not systemic absorption from a typical oral L-cysteine capsule/tablet, so this may not generalize to catalog L-cysteine products
The effect size is small and only marginally significant even in the larger, adequately-powered trial

excluded_pmids.reason: Systematic review of novel antibiofilm compounds for otitis media; does not confirm L-cysteine/NAC is among the specific compounds evaluated in the retrieved abstract text
Reviews AAMA, a urinary mercapturic-acid metabolite formed endogenously from acrylamide detoxification; this is an exposure biomarker for acrylamide, not an L-cysteine supplementation study
Systematic review of hangover treatments; the retrieved abstract text names clove extract as significant but does not confirm cysteine/NAC was among the tested interventions
Review of central venous catheter obstruction management (sodium hydroxide, etc.); no clear relation to L-cysteine supplementation
Review of commercial specimen-preservation products for tuberculosis diagnosis; unrelated to L-cysteine supplementation
Diagnostic biomarker review for head and neck cancer; S-carboxymethyl-L-cysteine appears only as a diagnostic salivary biomarker, not a treatment/supplement exposure

Pre-medication for endoscopic visibility; N-acetyl-L-cysteine was tested but found not to significantly improve visibility -- a procedural/clinical outcome unrelated to L-cysteine's typical marketed uses (antioxidant, respiratory, liver support)
Dietary supplements for prostate cancer; N-acetyl-L-cysteine appears only as one ingredient within a multi-component antioxidant/vitamin/mineral combination, not isolated
Cochrane review of cysteine/cystine/NAC added to PARENTERAL (IV) nutrition in neonates; wrong exposure route (not oral) and a clinical neonatal population
NAC used as a uroprotective agent against ifosfamide chemotherapy toxicity in sarcoma patients; an oncology-supportive-care context, not a general supplement efficacy claim
National Cancer Institute chemoprevention drug development strategy document listing NAC among 16 agents; a planning document, not a trial result
